title: Striking cash-secured puts in the money to keep upside
summary: If the market tends to rise, an in-the-money cash-secured put can make more than an out-of-the-money one. An in-the-money put equals a covered call struck just above the stock price, so it leaves room for appreciation. Roll or close before expiry to avoid assignment.

steps.caption: The stock trades at $100. We sell a 30-day put at $105, which is in the money.
Line A: the in-the-money put. It gains as the stock rises toward $105.
Line B: 100 shares plus a $105 call. The same shape: put-call parity makes the two trades equivalent.
Both keep about $5 of upside room from $100 to $105 before the gain is capped.
The difference is close to zero, only carry. The choice is strike location, not trade type.

takeaways: An in-the-money cash-secured put equals a covered call struck out of the money.
It leaves room for the stock to appreciate, which helps if the market's long-run upward bias holds.
Roll or close before expiration if you do not want assignment.
caveats: The 'more money over the long term' claim is the speaker's view and depends on a rising market.
Full downside of the stock remains; the backtest models it at stock-like risk.

backtest.note: Monthly cash-secured put struck in the money (60 delta); closed two days before expiry.
